entities.name: Diego Gelmírez
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Diego Gelmírez, who served as the second Bishop (1100–1120) and first Archbishop (1120–1140) of Santiago de Compostela, transformed a regional Galician see into a metropolitan archdiocese and a preeminent pilgrimage destination of medieval Europe. Born in the late 11th century, likely in Galicia, Gelmírez masterfully leveraged the burgeoning cult of Saint James the Greater to elevate his diocese's ecclesiastical and political standing throughout the Iberian Peninsula and beyond. His career, spanning four decades of intense political and religious maneuvering during the Reconquista, positioned Compostela as a powerful counterweight to Toledo and Braga, shaping the ecclesiastical geography of medieval Spain.

Gelmírez's episcopacy was marked by audacious territorial expansion and institutional consolidation. He successfully petitioned Pope Calixtus II, a personal friend, for Compostela's elevation to an archdiocese in 1120, granting it metropolitan authority over nine suffragan sees, including Mérida and Braga. He vigorously promoted the pilgrimage route, investing heavily in infrastructure, urban development, and the construction of the magnificent Romanesque cathedral, which became a beacon for pilgrims across Christendom. Furthermore, Gelmírez established a mint, organized a fleet to combat Norman and Saracen piracy along the Galician coast, and secured vast landholdings and fiscal privileges, effectively creating a quasi-independent ecclesiastical principality.

entities.name: Diego Gelmírez
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Diego Gelmírez (c. 1070 – January 22, 1140) was the transformative second bishop and first archbishop of Santiago de Compostela, a figure whose ecclesiastical and political acumen profoundly shaped the nascent Kingdom of Galicia and the broader Iberian Peninsula during the early 12th century. Operating from the burgeoning pilgrimage center of Santiago, Gelmírez masterfully elevated its status from a mere diocese to an archdiocese in 1120, securing papal recognition from Pope Calixtus II and positioning it as a spiritual and temporal rival to the ancient metropolitan see of Braga. His strategic vision for Compostela transcended religious administration, directly influencing the political landscape of León-Castile and leaving an indelible mark on medieval Spanish historiography through the *Historia Compostelana*, a unique biographical chronicle commissioned under his patronage.

Gelmírez's episcopacy, spanning from 1100 to 1139, was marked by relentless institutional expansion and territorial consolidation. He secured extensive land grants and privileges for his see, establishing a formidable temporal lordship that included minting coinage and raising an army, which he deployed to defend Compostela against Viking incursions and to assert influence over rival nobles and bishops. He initiated ambitious construction projects, most notably the completion and consecration of the Romanesque Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in 1128, a monumental achievement that cemented the city's role as a preeminent Christian pilgrimage destination. His diplomatic efforts saw him navigate complex relationships with Alfonso VI, Urraca, and Alfonso VII of León-Castile, often playing a pivotal role in succession disputes and regional power struggles.
